newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New crew faces Hydra of woes on Mir space station.
newsitem.headline: New crew faces Hydra of woes on Mir space station.

text.p: The new crew of cosmonauts bound for the stricken Mir space station faces an array of woes which, like the mythical Hydra, seems to sprout new problems as soon as earlier challenges are conquered.
On Tuesday, the current crew continued to tinker in vain with the Elektron oxygen generating system, which has not worked since late last week, space officials said.

"They were trying to turn it on last week and it turned itself off," NASA spokeswoman Kathleen Maliga said from Mission Control. "They're still working on it and they will keep working on it, well, until they get it back up over the next week."
The relief team of two Russian cosmonauts blasted off for Mir from the Baikonur launch pad in Kazakhstan on Tuesday. They were expected to reach Mir on Thursday.

The main focus of the mission for new commander Anatoly Solovyov and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov will be to repair the Spektr module, the former living quarters of U.S. astronauts aboard Mir, which collided with Mir's resupply ship on June 254.
It was the worst accident in the station's history.
The 12-metre (40-foot)-long Spektr is now sealed off from the rest of Mir and is dark and airless. Its solar panels are not gathering energy since the crew unplugged its cables after the accident.
On August 20 Vinogradov, a novice to space flight, will don a bulky spacesuit and open the Spektr's hatch for the first time in two months to reattach the cables to the solar panels.

With Solovyov assisting in the narrow workspace, he will also install a new hatch and attempt to repressurise the node linking Spektr to the rest of the ship after closing the hatch. If this repressurisation fails, they will have to abandon ship.
Experts also say that there may be jagged objects or dangerous chemicals floating inside Spektr. If something were to puncture a spacesuit, the cosmonaut would suffer instant death.

That repair is only the first of several needed to bring life back to Spektr, which was put into orbit in 1995. On September 3, Solovyov and Vinogradov will take a spacewalk to examine Spektr's external puncture, and only at a later date will they return to patch up the damage.

Success in reattaching the cables will restore much of the power Mir lost in the June 25 accident, although one of Spektr's four solar panels damaged in the collision is unrepairable, space officials say.
If the cosmonauts can later patch the exterior, they may be able to use some of the scientific tools inside as equipment to research the Earth's atmosphere.

But other problems could distract the cosmonauts before they finish working on Spektr. The current crew was preparing to undertake the repair job when the commander developed heart troubles and then a cosmonaut accidentally unplugged a vital computer, causing Mir to lose its orientation for more than a day.
Now the oxygen system is another example of a nagging woe that, though not an imminent danger, could eventually threaten the safety of the space station.
Mir has a back-up Elektron oxygen generating system but it is in the Kvant-2 module, which is shut off to conserve power until Spektr's solar energy panels are working again.
A third system which pumps out oxygen from the Progress supply ship is now used up, leaving just a two-month supply of oxygen-generating canisters, Maliga said.
Before his departure, Vinogradov was philosophical about the many problems, saying they came with exploring new frontiers.

"We are like babies in space, we've just started to work there," he told reporters on Monday. "We are only learning to work though we've been there for 40 years already. But these are only our first steps."
